report:
The evidence does not support "no" — it actually shows the opposite.

**Denosumab reduces vertebral fracture risk during active treatment.** The pivotal FREEDOM trial (NEJM, 2009), a 3-year randomized, placebo-controlled study of ~7,800 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found denosumab reduced new vertebral fractures by 68%, hip fractures by 40%, and nonvertebral fractures by 20% versus placebo (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). The 10-year FREEDOM Extension confirmed sustained low vertebral fracture rates and progressive BMD gains with continued treatment (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/). A large network meta-analysis (BMJ, 2023) comparing osteoporosis drugs likewise ranks denosumab among the most effective agents for reducing vertebral and hip fracture risk (https://www.bmj.com/content/381/bmj-2021-068033).

**The important caveat — and likely source of confusion — is discontinuation.** Stopping denosumab without transitioning to another antiresorptive causes a "rebound" surge in bone turnover, rapid BMD loss, and a markedly elevated risk of multiple vertebral fractures, sometimes exceeding pretreatment risk. This rebound effect has been documented in post-hoc FREEDOM analyses and multiple cohort studies (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jbmr.4705).

**Conclusion:** The premise that denosumab does not reduce vertebral fracture risk is incorrect. High-quality randomized trial evidence (FREEDOM) and network meta-analyses consistently show denosumab significantly lowers vertebral fracture risk while patients remain on therapy. The real clinical concern is not lack of efficacy but the rebound fracture risk after stopping the drug, which requires careful management (e.g., transitioning to a bisphosphonate) rather than reflecting a failure of denosumab to prevent fractures during treatment.
